title: Why highlighting feels more useful than it is
hook: Stop confusing feeling smart with actually learning.
cta: Save this for your next study session.

slides.label: Slide 1
slides.title: Why Highlighting Feels Useful
slides.body: It gives instant fluency and focus—but often not deeper learning.

slides.label: Slide 2
slides.title: The fluency illusion
slides.body: Seeing highlighted text increases familiarity; familiarity is mistaken for mastery.

slides.label: Slide 3
slides.title: Recognition vs. recall
slides.body: Highlighting supports recognition—later you recognize lines, but you can't produce the idea from memory.

slides.label: Slide 4
slides.title: Selective attention trap
slides.body: We tend to highlight vivid phrases or examples, not the underlying principle or how to use it.

slides.label: Slide 5
slides.title: Highlights become decorations
slides.body: Without testing, highlights turn into passive ornaments you reread instead of retrieving information.

slides.label: Slide 6
slides.title: Make highlights into cues
slides.body: Highlight one line per idea; write a short question in the margin; later cover text and answer from memory.

slides.label: Slide 7
slides.title: Takeaway: Use highlights smartly
slides.body: Highlights feel useful because they increase fluency. To learn, turn them into retrieval cues and practice active recall with spacing.
slides.footer: Discuss: How will you change your highlighting?

caption: Highlighting boosts fluency, not always learning. Use one-line highlights, write a margin question, then self-test and space reviews. Save this post and try it next study session.
